findings.title: Devotion expressed in care
findings.claim: Exclusive worship and care for parents form one ethical sequence: the Godward command continues into speech that protects the parents' dignity, and wider passages place the same pairing among obligations to other people.
findings.mechanism: In 12:40, judgment is assigned to God amid a dispute about worship, and exclusive worship is given as the commanded outcome. In 2:83, exclusive worship, parental goodness, and good speech to people occur within one covenant; 4:36 widens the recipients to kin, orphans, the poor, and neighbors, while 6:151 places parental goodness beside protection of children. These sequences contact the focus's decisive command, worship, and noble-word carriers. The counter-scene in 46:17 gives the small utterance of uff a concrete face-to-face form, and 93:10 carries the no-rebuke discipline to a petitioner. The focus's speech choices therefore become a social enactment of the prior allegiance.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive the connection in both directions: exclusive devotion frames the ethical order, while the treatment of a dependent parent makes that allegiance concrete in ordinary speech and opens the same ethic beyond kinship.
findings.containment: These passages are not identical, and parental care does not become worship. 29:8 keeps a boundary in view: parental goodness remains while pressure to associate partners is not obeyed. 49:13 places standing with God on piety rather than lineage, but does not make parental speech the measure of honor. The wider texts supply contextual parallels, not missing target-side morphology or lexical analysis.

epistemic.reason: The focus alignment is complete and the trusted cross-run publication supplies the integrated claim. Exact wider Arabic and connection notes ground the contextual contacts, while target morphology is absent and the resulting relation remains interpretive.

findings.title: Care through the life course
findings.claim: The parents' arrival at old age places the addressee beside those who once bore and raised them; wider life-course passages make this a transfer of care within the parent-child relation, while another scene keeps parental protection flowing toward children.
findings.mechanism: 46:15 recounts a mother's hardship in carrying and delivering a child, his growth to maturity, and his prayer of gratitude for his parents and concern for his offspring. That life course meets the focus's parents reaching old age at the addressee's side and changes aging from private decline into a relational handover. 18:82 depicts a father's earlier righteousness protecting orphan boys until they reach maturity, so the wider picture also retains parent-to-child protection. 19:8 presents old age as a bodily threshold beside barrenness and the wish for a son, adding a separate late-life contour.
findings.reader_payoff: The care demanded at parental old age can be seen as a return along a life of nurture, without making care flow in only one direction or making old age mean only dependency.
findings.containment: 46:15's maturity and forty-year thresholds are not declared identical to the parents' old age. 18:82 is a different protective act, not filial care for an elder; 19:8 is not a role-reversal scene. These wider images coexist with the focus's particular duty and do not establish a single chronology.

epistemic.reason: The trusted cross-run finding is anchored to the focus's parent, reaching, and age words. Exact wider Arabic and connection notes supply the life-course contacts, but target-side morphology is unavailable and the role-reversal relation is interpretive.

findings.title: Speech as social support
findings.claim: At the threshold of parental dependence, the focus treats speech as part of care: restraint from rebuke and a valued word keep a vulnerable person socially received, including when material help is delayed. The wider no-rebuke instruction to a petitioner carries that discipline beyond family relations.
findings.mechanism: The focus places parents in the addressee's presence at old age, prohibits a sharp rebuke, and then commands a noble word. 93:10 applies a no-rebuke rule to a person who asks, making refusal to drive someone away a wider form of social reception. 2:83 places good speech beside parental goodness, while 4:36 extends the ethical list to kin, orphans, the poor, and neighbors. These triggers meet the focus's rebuke and noble-word carriers and give the reader-walk's support inference an external social setting.
findings.reader_payoff: A good word becomes more than manners: it can preserve welcome and dignity when another person is dependent or asking, even when words cannot supply material aid.
findings.containment: The social-support reading is an abductive interpretation from legacy_unbound reader-walk evidence and exact wider parallels. The connections support restraint and good speech, but do not say that speech replaces provision or prove that material help is always delayed. The local support references do not serve as global triggers here.

epistemic.reason: The reader-walk explicitly marks its material-care link as an inference and is legacy_unbound. Supplied inter-surah Arabic and connection notes independently support the no-rebuke and good-speech contacts, while the claim about social support remains abductive.
